title: Facing injustice
hook: standing up for what is right, peacefully first
tomorrow: someone comments 'go back home' under Simran's photo. now what?

segments.voice: Yesterday, losing a job: honest work gone, and the sangat showing up with groceries and leads. Not alone. Today the trouble isn't money. It's someone being cruel, in public.

The bus stop, early, and the freshman in the navy patka is staring at his shoes. His name is Arjan; his family moved here this year. A junior keeps flicking the knot on top of his head while two friends film and laugh. Simran sees it from across the street, and her first thought is the loud one: drop the backpack, get in his face. She crosses. She stands right next to Arjan, holds up her own phone, and says, very calmly: stop. I'm recording too, and the vice principal gets both videos. The laughing stops. Then the bus pulls up, and nobody knows yet what happens next.
screen: `A FRESHMAN IN A NAVY PATKA.` → `HER FIRST THOUGHT: GET IN HIS FACE.` → `SHE STANDS NEXT TO HIM.` → `STOP. I'M RECORDING TOO.`

segments.voice: What Simran did has an old shape. Guru Nanak lived through an invasion. When Babur's army swept into the Punjab, the Guru didn't stay quiet. In hymns now in the Guru Granth Sahib, he names what he saw. On Ang 360 he even turns to God and asks, in paraphrase: there was so much beating that people cried out; did you feel no pain? On Ang 722 he says, again in paraphrase: Nanak speaks the word of truth, and will tell the truth at the time of truth. So standing up starts with naming the wrong, out loud, even to power. Here's the detail worth telling a friend tonight: that hymn about an invasion is addressed to Bhai Lalo, a carpenter in Sikh tradition. Truth about kings, sent to a working man. Generations later, Guru Gobind Singh writes the Zafarnama, a letter to the emperor Aurangzeb. One line in it says, in paraphrase, that when every other means has failed, it is right to take up the sword. Look at the order in that sentence. Every other means comes first. Force is the last door, never the first one. So facing injustice has a sequence: see it, stand beside the person it's hurting, name it plainly, and make sure the people who can act will hear. Peacefully first.
screen: `GURU NANAK NAMES WHAT HE SAW.` · `TRUTH, AT THE TIME OF TRUTH.` · `EVERY OTHER MEANS COMES FIRST.` · `SEE IT, STAND BESIDE, NAME IT.` · then, large: `STAND UP.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you've watched happen that wasn't fair, at school, at work, or online. Say out loud, in one plain sentence, what you'd say next time, something like: stop, that's not okay. Say it again, slower and calmer each time, until it sounds like your own voice.
Facing injustice. Seeing a wrong, standing beside the person it's hurting, and naming it out loud, peacefully first.
Hold onto this: stand up, with words first, the way Guru Nanak named what he saw. Day 1723, and Arjan wasn't alone at the bus stop.

screen: `DAY 1723 COUNTS.` → `LIVING IT · 97 OF 134.` → `TOMORROW: 'GO BACK HOME' UNDER SIMRAN'S PHOTO. NOW WHAT?`

howItsDone: Sikhs often point to the Gurus as people who named injustice openly, and some Sikh groups today speak up for people being harassed, through words, schools and the courts.

fork.setup: a group chat is piling a cruel nickname on a classmate who isn't in it. going by today, what's the first move?
options: post one plain line, 'stop, that's not okay,' and tell someone who can act.
screenshot it all and post it publicly to shame them right back.
stay out of it for now, and speak up only if it gets physical.
fork.reveal: see it, stand beside the person, name it plainly, let the right people hear: the sequence Guru Nanak's hymns and the Zafarnama point to. peacefully first.

original.note: Gurmukhi: sach, truth. Guru Nanak will tell the truth at the time of truth (Ang 722).

trapdoor: what you thought: standing up means fighting back, harder than they did.
what it means: name the wrong, stand beside the person, and use every peaceful means first.
what a scholar hears: the Babarvani hymns (Ang 360; Ang 722-723, addressed to Lalo) name Babur's violence; the Zafarnama allows the sword only when all other means have failed.
guess: seeing a wrong and naming it out loud, peacefully first
staying calm and saying nothing so it all blows over
getting even with anyone who hurts your own people
recall: not alone: the sangat shows up

chat.says: ok i didn't shove him. but part of me really wanted to. was calm the weak move?
options: no. Guru Nanak named wrongs out loud; every other means comes first.
yes. with bullies, only a shove gets the message through, honestly.
calm only works if a teacher is standing right there to back you.
chat.meaning: Guru Nanak named the wrong to power, and the Zafarnama puts every other means before force. Calm, out loud, beside him: that's standing up.

patka.meaning: a small cloth head covering some Sikh boys wear

Babur.meaning: the invader whose army swept into the Punjab in Guru Nanak's time

Ang.meaning: a page of the Guru Granth Sahib

Bhai Lalo.meaning: Guru Nanak's friend, a carpenter in Sikh tradition

Zafarnama.meaning: Guru Gobind Singh's letter to the emperor Aurangzeb

sources.ref: Ang 360, Asa, Guru Nanak (Babarvani: 'eti maar pai kurlaane tain ki dard na aaia'), paraphrased
Ang 722-723, Tilang, Guru Nanak (addressed to Lalo: 'sach ki baani Nanak aakhai, sach sunaaisi sach ki bela'), paraphrased
Zafarnama, Guru Gobind Singh (the couplet on taking up the sword when all other means have failed), paraphrased

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 written: shape story (Simran steps in at the bus stop; the teach answers what she did with Guru Nanak's Babarvani and the Zafarnama).
For parents: the hook shows a younger boy's patka being flicked and filmed; the teach mentions an invasion's beating in one line. Kept gentle, no graphic detail.
Confirm Ang 360 (Asa M1, 'eti maar pai kurlaane, tain ki dard na aaia') and the paraphrase.

Confirm Ang 722-723 (Tilang M1, addressed to Lalo) for 'sach ki baani Nanak aakhai, sach sunaaisi sach ki bela' and the paraphrase. Lalo as a carpenter is from Sikh tradition (janamsakhis); the voice says so.

Confirm the Zafarnama couplet (often numbered 22: chu kar az hama heelte dar guzasht...) and the paraphrase 'when every other means has failed, it is right to take up the sword.' The voice says 'generations later' rather than a count.

Storyline (1723-1736): Arjan, a Sikh freshman whose family recently arrived, is mocked at the bus stop; Simran stands up for him; the school process, waiting, a partial outcome; then week two: welcoming Arjan's family as newcomers, neighbors of other faiths (Mrs. Haddad next door), the boy who mocked him gets hurt, smoke days, and a shared garden with Bebe.
2026-10-15: new lesson recipe data (chat, gloss, recall) written with the lesson (job 3 recipe); confirm the chat reply, glosses, scripts and pronunciations with the Keeper.
